newsitem.title: USA: Wheat leads grain price fall, gasoline prices firm.
newsitem.headline: Wheat leads grain price fall, gasoline prices firm.

text.p: Slower export prospects pushed wheat prices lower Thursday and gasoline prices remained firm on worries about low stockpiles and refinery problems.

At the Chicago Board of Trade speculators sold from the opening bell after world wheat supplies were estimated to grow, European export subsidies for wheat expanded and weekly export sales reported by the Department of Agriculture were much lower than expected.
December wheat fell 14-1/2 cents to $3.84 a bushel.

Grain exporters said European Union officials in Brussels had awarded wheat export subsidies on sales of 290,000 metric tons of wheat, raising competition another notch between the U.S. and European producers.
"The world market is weak. The European Union stepped up their restitution to ... double" last week's subsidy, said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures.
The government also reported U.S. net wheat exports for the week ended Oct. 17 were only 279,500 metric tons, down 62 percent from a week ago.
The London-based International Grains Council also boosted its estimate for 1996 world wheat production to 573 million metric tons from the previous 571 million.
December corn fell 4-3/4 cents to $2.78 a bushel after weekly exports came in at 220,200 metric tons, 74 percent below the previous week.
Soybeans also finished lower as speculators sold off grains but buying from commercial grain companies and brighter export prospects aided that market, traders said.
November soybeans ended down two cents a bushel at $6.96-1/2 after a trading as high as $7.07.

Net exports of soybeans for the week were strong at nearly 1.4 million metric tons, 20 percent above last week's marketing year high and only six percent less than weekly record of 1,484,300 tons for a week in November 1987.
Traders said the market took notice of not only the weekly sales tally but were encouraged by the 287,800 tons sold to China and a sale of 331,600 tons to unknown destinations.
"Obviously we're firm on the sales number. The pace of usage coupled with the China sales and sales to unknown puts us ahead of last year's pace," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices rose on talk of refinery problems but crude and heating oil prices fell after indications supply concerns were easing.
November unleaded gasoline rose 1.06 cents a gallon to 69.22 cents.
Market talk that refiners were seeking gasoline supplies from the cash markets sparked rumours that they were suffering mechanical problems or outages.
"The big thing today was that Exxon, Chevron and Texaco were seen in the cash market," said one NYMEX trader.

The American Petroleum Institute said on Tuesday that U.S. gasoline stocks fell nearly six million barrels in the week ended October 18, while crude oil stocks rose 5.7 million barrels and heating oil stocks grew 2.4 million barrels.
November heating oil ended down 0.47 cent at 70.49 cents a gallon and December crude fell 35 cents a barrel to $24.51.
"I think a major effort is a afoot to boost distillate stocks and given the high production of distillate, the fear is that gasoline will suffer," said Steve Platt, an analyst with Dean Witter.
Distillate is the basic feedstock for producing heating oil, which has been at historically low levels ahead of winter especially in the Northeast.
